articles.title_orig: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.title_zh: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.content_orig:
Ricardo Gonzalez was injured and taken to hospital after confrontation in Long Beach, according to officials
Federal immigration agents broke the arm of a US citizen in what a Democratic congressman said was a “brutal attack” during a confrontation with protesters in California.
Video of Saturday’s encounter in Long Beach shows Ricardo Gonzalez, identified as a former city employee, handcuffed and face down in a gutter, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officers kneeling on his back.
Rex Richardson, Long Beach’s mayor, told CNN on Sunday that Gonzalez had called emergency responders for help at one point. In an online fundraiser for his medical expenses, Gonzalez’s daughter, Leslie, said he was knocked off his e-bike by an unmarked ICE vehicle.
“He was tased twice, pinned to the ground, and taken to the hospital for serious injuries,” Leslie’s fundraiser said. “What ICE did was not right.”
Richardson said: “When the police arrived, we know that he was detained. He was on a curb. He was injured.”
The episode centering on Gonzalez is the latest in a number of recent violent and sometimes deadly encounters involving federal officers conducting enforcement actions as part of Donald trump’s immigration crackdown.
The homeland security department, which oversees ICE, has not commented publicly on why Gonzalez was detained. But it frequently portrays its agents’ actions as self-defense or protecting public safety.
The Guardian has contacted ICE for comment.
Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat who represents Long Beach, posted on X that he was disturbed by the encounter and called for the abolition of ICE.
“ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and US citizen,” he wrote.
“The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country. I’m proud of the neighbors who documented and stood up for the family being terrorized by ICE.
“Donald Trump and his inhumane and illegal deportation machine must be stopped. Long Beach stands with our community and our immigrant families.”
In a statement , the Long Beach police department (LBPD) said ICE personnel also called for emergency assistance “due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical aid”. The LBPD statement also said officers arrived to find “a large group disturbance” taking place involving the federal agents.
“One officer located a handcuffed male adult, being detained by ICE, who was bleeding,” the statement said. “Officers transported the handcuffed injured man to a nearby fire station. There, LBPD personnel removed the handcuffs and LBFD personnel transported the man to the hospital for medical attention.”
The LBPD said it was not involved in any immigration enforcement action and made no arrests. It said ICE agents who followed officers into a secure parking lot “were subsequently directed to leave the station”.
“They were later advised that if they wanted to file a vandalism report, they could contact the City of Long Beach Communications Center,” the LBPD statement added.
The Gonzalez case in Long Beach has parallels with an incident in Texas on 10 October in which an ICE agent driving an unmarked SUV ran over a man and broke his leg in three places .
Harris county, Texas, district attorney Sean Teare said he was considering bringing felony assault charges against the immigration officer after video appeared to show the vehicle swerving into the man in a parking lot in the Houston area.
At a news conference on Friday, Houston-based advocacy group FIEL accused ICE of crashing into that man while searching for another who had died years earlier. A FIEL official told the Associated Press it had turned over to Teare a death certificate for the man the group says ICE was apparently looking for.
ICE on Friday did not respond to AP’s questions about the matter.

articles.title_orig: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.title_zh: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.content_orig:
Metro workers repair tracks damaged in a Russian attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 19, 2026. (Chris Occhicone/The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Later on Oct. 19, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said more than 70 workers were repairing the damaged metro infrastructure, with the most difficult work involving power supply and train control systems. Repairs had continued since overnight but were being slowed by air raid alerts, which forced crews to take shelter.
Train service between Lisova and Akademmistechko stations was expected to resume that evening, with trains skipping Chernihivska until repairs were completed, Klitschko added.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
The Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center sustained significant damage in the Solomianskyi District. Its administration said no employees were injured and that the mall was working to resume operations as soon as possible. The center did not disclose the extent of the damage or provide a timeline for repairs.
Serhii Misan, 68, a local resident, had planned to pick up his new refrigerator from Cosmo Multimall on the morning of Oct. 19.
"I only paid for a refrigerator yesterday, and they told me I could pick it up today," Misan said. "And now look at what's happening here."
"(The Russians) are terrorists. They strike civilian targets. They spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They just kill civilians."
Misan added that, in light of recent developments, Ukraine would struggle to resist Russia without a strong partner like the U.S.
"If aid is reduced, it will be very difficult to stand up to an aggressor like Russia," he said. "We are not trying to seize their land. We are trying to defend our right to live freely on our own land."
Sofiia Kelli, 18, who lives in the Solomianskyi district, told The Kyiv Independent that her apartment was also damaged in the Russian attack on the capital. Her family was only able to take shelter in an underground parking garage after the attack began, as there was too little time between the air raid alert and the strikes.
"It was a huge shock. It was extremely loud — nothing like the other explosions we've heard in our neighborhood," Kelli said.
"I couldn't fall asleep afterward. Then I just sat in the bathroom and cried for a very long time. It's hard to process everything that happened because you always think something like this won't happen to you. And then it does."
"They [Russians] strike civilian targets. They [Russians] spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They [Russians] just kill civilians."
Kelli said she intends to stay in Kyiv despite the latest attack and is getting ready for the coming winter.
"Everything depends on electricity. Of course, it's difficult, but we're doing the best we can. We've installed solar panels (on the building) and a generator to keep the elevators running," she added.
Klitschko also reported damage to a medical center in the same district. The blast wave shattered more than 200 windows, damaged doors and ceilings, and damaged medical equipment, he said.
No medical center staff were injured, and there were no patients inside the facility at the time of the attack.
The Russian attack also destroyed a data center operated by telecommunications company Datagroup, which provides electronic communications services to users in more than 90 settlements across Ukraine.
The company said the facility's equipment and infrastructure had been damaged beyond repair. No employees were injured in the attack.
Russian attacks also hit settlements in Kyiv Oblast surrounding the capital. In Irpin, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Kyiv, one woman was killed and 19 people were injured, including nine children.
At around 9 a.m. local time, Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said that three people were missing. Search operations are ongoing, he added.
The Russian strikes damaged 70 houses, five apartment buildings, industrial facilities, and warehouses in Irpin, according to Tkachenko.
Recent ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv have arrived with little or no advance warning amid deteriorating relations between Ukraine and the U.S., which provides intelligence used to track Russian missile launches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on the morning of Oct. 19 that Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, adding that Kyiv had received no advance warning from its partners about the launches.
According to Zelensky, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region being the primary targets.
"When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners," Zelensky wrote on X.
"The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia's desire to drag this war out."
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Ukrainian Air Force's communications department, said on national television that Russia launched two waves of ballistic missile attacks overnight on Oct. 19, at around 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. local time.
Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners ahead of the first wave, but information about the second wave was provided, Ihnat said.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
"Information was indeed not provided the first time, for certain reasons. Our experts are looking into this together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred. Information was provided at 3 a.m.," Ihnat said.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened."
Commenting on Ukrainian officials' claims that partners had not provided advance warning of Russia's ballistic missile launches overnight, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on the morning of Oct. 19 that he "did not know exactly" what had happened.
"I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving (Ukrainian) early warning system," Rubio said.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back.  I can't comment on what happened last night," he added.

Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Phone alerts went off moments before the blasts, while the street sirens began "howling during the explosions," Chief Editor Olga Rudenko reported.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.

Per GM’s announcement , a very limited rollout started in late September, and is expanding throughout October before hitting more vehicles in December.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia to postpone in-person ‘Davos in the desert’ event after Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia to postpone in-person ‘Davos in the desert’ event after Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks.
The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29.
The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured.
The conference organizers said in an email that they will communicate new dates for the event soon. Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference.
They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sach's David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink, and Citigroup's Jane Fraser among others.
CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference  has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017.

articles.title_orig: Israeli Police Detain 10 Over Violent Settler Attacks in West Bank
articles.title_zh: Israeli Police Detain 10 Over Violent Settler Attacks in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
ABU SNIN, Israel — Israeli police said they arrested 10 people on Monday in connection with a wave of settler violence that included attacks on a foreign journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank over the weekend.
Israel had come under heavy international criticism for the attacks. Israeli police did not identify the suspects or specify their roles in the attacks, which came during a spike in settler violence during the annual Palestinian olive harvest season.
On Friday, Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten by a crowd of young male settlers, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae in the village of Abu Falah. She also underwent surgery on a finger that was nearly severed and is recovering from what appeared to be stab wounds to her lower body, which required stitches.
A day later, masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and others visiting the Christian village of Taybeh.
Settler violence has surged in recent years, and rights groups say that attackers are rarely arrested or punished for attacks on Palestinians.
From her hospital bed Sunday, Levine said she was “shocked and insulted” that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cast doubt on the attack, which was witnessed by a crowd of people, by calling it “alleged.”
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee condemned the attack as a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards” and said they should spend years in prison. Israel’s president and several opposition politicians also spoke out against the attack.
The attack on diplomats targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives.
“Impunity for violent settlers must end,” Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said afterward.
Israeli police said they have been collecting evidence and witness statements since the weekend attacks. The suspects were transferred for questioning. They said the Shin Bet internal security agency, the paramilitary border police force and the Israeli military had all participated in the investigation.
Police said Monday’s operation also targeted people suspected of violating military orders declaring a closed military zone and offenses involving illegal construction. They said they seized several vehicles and items linking suspects to alleged offenses.
Saeed writes for the Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: New nonstop Lufthansa flight announced from Columbus to Frankfurt
articles.title_zh: New nonstop Lufthansa flight announced from Columbus to Frankfurt
articles.content_orig:
Published: October 19, 2026
(COLUMBUS) The Columbus Regional Airport Authority, Lufthansa Airlines, JobsOhio and One Columbus today announced that Central Ohio's first nonstop flight to Europe will launch in May 2027, connecting John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) with Frankfurt Airport (FRA) in Germany. The new service marks a major milestone for the Columbus Region and Ohio, providing direct access to one of the world's leading international hubs and creating new opportunities for businesses, travelers and visitors throughout the state.
“Today's announcement is a tremendous milestone for the Columbus Region and Ohio,” said Daren Griffin, CRAA President and CEO. “Lufthansa's new nonstop service to Frankfurt provides our passengers with a direct link to one of the world's strongest global networks, enhancing connectivity, competitiveness and continued growth. We are grateful to Lufthansa, JobsOhio, One Columbus, our business community and so many others whose partnership helped make this opportunity possible. At a time of extraordinary transformation for our airports and our region, this new service establishes Ohio's gateway to continental Europe. It strengthens our state's connections to the global economy and creates new opportunities for communities across Ohio. We couldn't be more excited about what it means for our businesses, travelers and the future of Ohio”
This will be Ohio's first and only nonstop flight to Germany, serving hundreds of daily passengers from Columbus and across Ohio who travel to Europe each day. Lufthansa will operate the service with a Boeing 787 Dreamliner featuring the airline's Allegris cabin experience, including 28 lie-flat business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 economy seats, for a total of 287 seats.
“We are very pleased to connect Columbus and the state of Ohio directly with our Frankfurt hub, the first intercontinental flight from this great city,” said Dirk Janzen, Lufthansa Group Vice President of Passenger Sales, the Americas. “The new service will provide both business and leisure travelers with a convenient nonstop connection to Germany, as well as onward destinations across our Lufthansa Group network. The launch of this route is an important step in our continued expansion in the United States, our most important market outside the Lufthansa Group’s home markets. We look forward to strengthening the connections between Ohio and Europe, and to welcoming travelers from Columbus and the surrounding region,” Janzen added.
The flight will provide unprecedented connectivity for the 38 German-based companies operating in the Columbus Region and further support all German companies investing in Ohio and employing thousands of Ohioans across the state. Through Lufthansa's Frankfurt hub, travelers will have convenient access to more than 130 destinations across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India.
The new service is also expected to make it easier for international visitors, investors and talent to access the Columbus Region and explore opportunities across Ohio, further supporting the state's economic development efforts.
“Ohio is committed to building a collaborative partnership with Lufthansa to support the success of this new route and strengthen the significant ties that benefit both of our regions,” said Ohio Governor Mike DeWine. “This new route will be transformative, giving our state access to critical markets in Germany, Europe and the world while establishing stronger economic, research, cultural and educational exchanges.”
Germany is the third-largest source of international investment in Ohio, behind only Japan and Canada. More than 750 German-owned business establishments operate in Ohio, second only to Japan, according to the Ohio Department of Development, and German companies support approximately 41,000 jobs across the state, according to the Transatlantic Economy 2025 report. Ohio businesses also exported nearly $1.4 billion in goods to Germany in 2023. Overall, Ohio ranks third in the nation for foreign direct investment, with about 4,000 companies from 42 countries operating in the state.
The new route builds on the success of JobsOhio’s Air Service Restoration program, which works with airports, regional partners and airlines to establish routes that are important to economic development. JobsOhio created the program after businesses and stakeholders said during a 2019 statewide listening tour that air service at Ohio airports had declined more sharply than in competitor states. Through the program, JobsOhio and regional partners share revenue guarantees that reduce the risk for airlines launching new service.
Since 2020, it has helped bring 32 new routes and 15 route expansions with six airlines to five Ohio airports, adding more than 590,000 new seats and more than 187,000 additional seats each year and generating an estimated $230 million in annual economic impact. JobsOhio has committed $36.8 million in revenue guarantees, alongside $10.1 million from local partners.
“Businesses, including the German companies that employ tens of thousands of Ohioans, tell us that better air service is essential to investing and creating jobs in Ohio,” said JobsOhio President and CEO J.P. Nauseef. “We listened, and this direct link to Frankfurt is exactly what our Air Service Restoration program was built to deliver.”
The new air service comes as the Columbus Region experiences some of the strongest economic growth in the country. The Columbus metro leads the Midwest in job creation, adding nearly 12,000 jobs between March 2025 and March 2026, with a growth rate more than 18 times the national average. The Region’s population also grew by more than 21,000 residents in 2025, twice the national growth rate. The new international connection is expected to further strengthen the Region’s ability to attract businesses, investment and talent from around the world.
“The Columbus Region is in the middle of an extraordinary stretch of job creation and business investment, and now we’re adding direct access to one of Europe’s most important business hubs,” said Jonas Peterson, Chief Economic Development Officer and President of One Columbus. “That’s a significant competitive advantage. It makes it easier for global companies to invest here, strengthens connections for businesses already operating in our Region and improves our ability to compete for the next major project. We have tremendous economic momentum right now, and this new connection gives us an opportunity to accelerate it even further.”
The Columbus Region continues to attract global investment and advanced industries, including recent commitments from companies such as Anduril, Intel and Bayer. The new Lufthansa service further strengthens Ohio's position as a destination for business growth and international commerce.
The CMH-FRA route will begin operating in May 2027, with bookings available beginning Tuesday, Oct. 20. Service will operate three times weekly on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. Flights will depart Columbus at 4:20 p.m. and arrive in Frankfurt at 6:15 a.m. (local times).
The Lufthansa Group is a globally operating aviation group, with more than 100,000 employees worldwide. It is Europe's largest airline group by revenue, generating revenue of EUR 39.6 billion (EUR 39,597 million) in the 2025 financial year. The Lufthansa Group comprises mulitple business segments, including Passenger Airlines, Logistics, Technology (Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul), as well as other companies and group functions, including IT services and Lufthansa Aviation Training.
The Lufthansa Group’s portfolio of airlines includes Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, ITA Airways, Eurowings and Discover Airlines, connecting customers to destinations around the globe. articles.title_zh: Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov, 51, OBM
articles.content_orig:
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a beloved educator and longtime member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday, 8 Cheshvan, 5787.
Rabbi Malov suffered a sudden cardiac arrest shortly after waking up and washing Negel Vasser. Emergency responders were called to his home but were unable to revive him.
His sudden passing has shocked the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad and his many friends and acquaintances throughout Israel and around the world.
Rabbi Malov served as the Rebbe’s Shliach in Kfar HaRif and dedicated much of his life to Jewish education. For many years, he directed the neighborhood’s evening yeshiva program, where hundreds of children gathered nightly in the local shul to study Torah.
Friends described him as a devoted educator and accomplished Torah scholar, knowledgeable in both Nigleh and Chassidus, who worked tirelessly to spread Torah learning.
He also organized annual Kinusei Torah in the neighborhood around Yom Tov, in accordance with the Rebbe’s directive to hold Torah gatherings during the holidays.
Rabbi Malov was the son-in-law of Rabbi Yitzchak Yehuda Yeruslavsky , Rov of Nachlas Har Chabad and a leading Chabad Rov.
He was born in Bnei Brak to Rabbi Tzvi Eliyahu Malov , OBM, a longtime Chabad communal activist in Yerushalayim who passed away approximately six years ago, and Mrs. Chana Chaya Malov , daughter of R’ Yaakov Moshe Hakohen Halperin , who passed away in Tishrei 5751 at the age of 40.
He is survived by his wife, Mrs. Nechama Dina Malov , and their children: Menachem Mendel, Shterna Sarah Kramer, Devorah Leah , and Mushka .
The levaya will depart from his home in Nachlas Har Chabad at 12:30 PM, passing the local Talmud Torah and central shul before proceeding to Shamgar in Yerushalayim.
The levaya will depart Shamgar at 3:00 PM for burial at Har Hamenuchos in Yerushalayim.

Jingle Jangle is about to be sold out in even more stores.
Trader Joe’s — home of infamous seasonal treats like Apple Cider Donuts , Pumpkin-Flavored Joe-Joe’s and the Christmas favorite Jingle Jangle — has announced more locations are on the way.
The nation’s favorite grocery chain recently announced on its website that shoppers will see even more stores — over 30. The new locations will be in the following three cities and will likely open in 2027:
The move comes after the California-based company revealed 25 new spots were coming across 14 states.
Some recent openings include West Palm Beach, Fla., on June 12, the New Orleans, La., location on June 10 and the Tucson, Ariz., location on May 29.
As of Oct. 12, the fan-favorite grocery chain revealed it will open the following:
Trader Joe’s did not set an opening date for the new locations, but it did tell Nexstar that locations marked as “opening soon” typically open three to six months after announcing them online.
The newest spot open to the public is in Reading, MA, as shoppers could start browsing aisles on Oct. 14.
In fact, TJ’s has kept up a fairly steady growth rate, opening 34 stores in 2024 and 43 stores in 2025.
The grocery chain currently has over 600 storefronts, but there are still states without a location, including Alaska, Hawaii, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, West Virginia and Wyoming.

Oops, something went wrong
Amazon ( AMZN ) stock rose more than 3% in early trading on Monday after Morgan Stanley named it a top pick and raised its price target to $350 from $335, outlining five catalysts that could drive the stock higher.
The new target implies about 40% upside from Friday's close of $250. With a bear case of $220 a share and a bull case of $410, the firm sees a 3:1 risk-reward ratio.
"In a market of see-sawing AI leaders and laggards, we detail 5 catalysts ahead to re-rate shares and drive material outperformance," analyst Brian Nowak, who kept his Overweight rating, wrote in a note Sunday.
Faster AWS growth: Morgan Stanley now expects revenue at AWS, Amazon's cloud unit, to grow 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, up from 41% and 37%. The change follows Nvidia's ( NVDA ) disclosure that it expects AWS to buy and deploy about 2 million of its GPUs over those two years. The extra chips also lift the firm's capital spending forecast for Amazon to $355 billion in 2027 and $365 billion in 2028.
Bigger AWS profits: Nowak expects AWS operating margins of 42% in 2027 and 44% in 2028, which supports about $16.50 in Amazon earnings per share in 2028.
Bedrock: More visibility into Bedrock, Amazon's AI model service, could lift the stock's valuation from about 15 times 2028 earnings, according to the note.
AI shopping: Nowak expects Amazon to emerge as a winner as AI shopping agents spread and expects it to partner over time with Meta's ( META ) Muse AI agent . The holiday season is the first big test.
Robotics: Every 10% of Amazon's global units that move through its robotics-enabled fulfillment centers could save $2 billion to $4 billion a year, Morgan Stanley estimates. The firm calls robotics a 2027 catalyst.
Amazon stock is up about 11% this year but sits roughly 10% below its early August high. Earlier this month, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi noted that Amazon was trading at one of its lowest trailing price-to-earnings ratios in years . Morgan Stanley's $350 target is based on about 21 times its 2028 earnings estimate.
Amazon reports third quarter results on Oct. 29 after the bell.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.content_orig:
Yemen's Saudi-backed government claimed Monday to have killed 558 Houthi fighters over the past 24 hours. In a post on X , Col. Majed Al-Nazili said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,164 operations against the Iran-backed rebels.
"The operations resulted in neutralizing (558) militia elements, including field commanders," he wrote.
A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told the French news agency AFP on Monday, amid repeated attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels .
One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organizers "won't announce a new date soon." A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, told AFP: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"
Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum often referred to as "Davos in the desert." The event typically draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is  scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the conference would either be held online or postponed.
Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.
"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.
He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.
Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.
Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA , al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighbouring Hadramout and Aden.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attacks the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.
Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a  "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.
Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.
The prices fell after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine , with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.
Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East .
On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.
A tug boat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday .
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."
"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."
Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.
The U.S. issued a security alert on Monday urging Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the statement said.
It added that hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly and that groups backed by Iran may target U.S. interests overseas "or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world."
At least 20 people, including one American, were killed in one week in October when Houthi rebels attacked Saudi airports.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was expected to pay his first visit to Iran on Monday since the U.S. and Israel sparked the ongoing war with the Islamic Republic by launching joint strikes on Feb. 28.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Sunday that the two sides would discuss "regional and international developments," while Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war."
Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Iran presented a seven-day ceasefire proposal in late September that called for an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a return to direct negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program. President Trump rejected the proposal, which Iran says remains on the table.
Conflict raged between the Houthis and the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Iran-backed rebel group on Sunday, as both sides traded strikes.

articles.title_orig: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.title_zh: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.content_orig:
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.
Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.
In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.
The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.
Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.
The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

articles.title_orig: 10 Mini Gadgets Worth 3D Printing Instead Of Buying
articles.title_zh: 10 Mini Gadgets Worth 3D Printing Instead Of Buying
articles.content_orig:
If you're thinking about buying a 3D printer , you should know that there's no limit to the things that you can make once you get one. While everyone has probably thought about making large pieces, printing smaller items could also result in lots of saved time and money.
For this article, we identified 10 mini gadgets worth 3D printing instead of buying, and we've given some examples for each of them so you can see the benefits. Some of our selections for this roundup include stands and docks for mobile devices, an alternative to keychains, and accessories for tabletop games.
All of the examples that we've included are publicly available from the best sites for free 3D printing projects , though some of them come with the restriction that you can only make them for personal use. They've all been downloaded at least 1,000 times, though, so it's likely the creators have received plenty of feedback and maybe even updated their files as needed to address any concerns raised.
When you buy an Apple Watch , there's no charging stand that comes with it. You'll only get a charging puck, so the smartwatch lies flat on your desk. You can buy a charging stand that holds the watch upright so that you can see the time and notifications, but most options in the market are expensive because they come with extras like wireless charging capabilities or additional space for your iPhone and AirPods. 3D printing this gadget will not only save on costs, but you'll also be able to choose the color that you want.
If you want something simple, there are 3D-printed options like the Apple Watch Charging Stand by Dan_ID on Maker World. With about 59,500 downloads, it holds the smartwatch's charging puck and sets the Apple Watch horizontally with the straps wrapped around it to minimize the space that it occupies on your desk.
Pulsar Designs' Charging Stand for Apple Watch , also available on Maker World and with 13,300 downloads, sets the wearable device vertically instead. This design also holds the charging puck securely, and it's compact while also elevating the smartwatch for a better look at the straps that you chose for the day.
Similar to the Apple Watch charging stand, a phone dock will allow you to see your smartphone's screen at all times, whether it's plugged into its charger or not. These accessories come in all shapes and sizes, but 3D printing one will allow you to choose the exact style that you want depending on how much space you have available on your desk and the size of your phone.
The Phone Stand by GoAftens on Thingiverse is as simple as it gets for this type of accessory. With about 40,100 downloads and originally made for Apple's iPhone 6, it has a hole at the bottom to allow a charging cable to plug into your phone while it's placed vertically on the stand, though you also have the option of setting it horizontally. You can adjust the width of the ledge if you've got a thick phone, such as a foldable, or because your preferred case is bulky.
Moss 3D's Adjustable Phone Stand , which has about 2,500 downloads on Maker World, is a slightly more modern version of the gadget. It's foldable for portability, and you can set it at a variety of angles to suit your needs. It features a locking function to keep it in place even when it's holding a heavier device like a tablet. With its retro aesthetic and your choice of colors for its parts, this phone stand also has more personality than many of the other options in the market.
Toothpaste squeezers are essential for frugal living, and it goes against the principles of the lifestyle if the gadget that you buy costs a lot, breaks easily, or isn't effective. 3D-printed toothpaste squeezers are not only tried and tested, but you'll also be able to make the exact number that you need, in the specific size for your usual toothpaste tubes.
The Toothpaste Squeezer by mgm86, which has been downloaded 28,500 times from Maker World, gives a more precise and direct squeeze than many similar gadgets that have a fixed slot. To use it, you remove the colored cap to insert the toothpaste tube, then re-insert the cap to tighten the grip and further flatten the tube. There are two sizes available for the project, one with a slot length of 58 millimeters and the other at 68 millimeters. You can also customize the colors of the caps depending on the household member who's using each particular brand of toothpaste.
The Ultimate Toothpaste Squeezer by the pro is another option, but it uses rollers to get every drop out of the tube instead of relying on direct pressure from your hands. Downloaded about 20,000 times on Printables, this gadget has a wheel for turning the gears and squeezing the toothpaste tube. It may look complicated, but assembly after 3D printing won't require additional tools, and it can be disassembled for thorough cleaning if necessary.
There are a lot of types of fidget toys you can buy , as they've evolved from just being simple spinners. You can now also click and squeeze them, among many other actions, with the goal of either keeping your mind focused or relieving your stress. If you're still figuring out what kind of fidget toy works the best for you, or if you already know and you want different versions of your favorites, you can 3D print them so that you can customize their size and colors.
Kriswillcode's Mechanical Switch Fidget Click Toy , which has 1,600 downloads on Thingiverse, mimics the feel and sound of typing on a mechanical keyboard. In addition to seven 3D-printed pieces that need to be accurately sized, you'll need a spring like those in retractable pens to assemble this gadget. If done right, you'll get a satisfying click each time you press its button.
For a different kind of fidget toy, there's the Tactile Fidget Rings by GlennovitS 3D. You can get its files from Printables, where it has been downloaded about 42,000 times. This is a print-in-place project, which means there's no assembly necessary after 3D printing, and there are a total of five options for the textures of the rotating rings. There are also four mixed versions that have a different texture for each ring, and of course, you can choose the color that you want when you print them for yourself or to give to your friends and family members.
Open bag clips are very useful in the kitchen, as they help keep food and ingredients fresh by allowing you to reseal the packages. However, when you buy these accessories, they usually come in bundles of different sizes, where some are too big or small, or there are so many that you won't be able to use them all. If you 3D print your open bag clips instead, you're going to get the specific size and quantity that you need, and you can even make them part of a color-coded system in your refrigerator or pantry.
The Crazy Crocodile Clip , made by Newstream and downloaded about 5,700 times on Maker World, is a 3D-printable open bag clip that resembles a crocodile, as its name suggests. It's more than just a fun design, though, as the accessory can keep packages sealed securely. This latest version of the project has a stronger print-in-place hinge for durability than earlier iterations, and as its creator suggested, it can even double as a fidget toy.
Coffee Clip for Open Bags , which has about 24,000 downloads on Printables, adds a resealable cap to the open bag clip for easy pouring of whatever's inside. Pressi, the designer of the 3D-printed gadget, said that it can be used for coffee beans, snacks, spices, and other similar food items in lightweight packages.
If you're always misplacing your keys, a key organizer can help make sure that they're all in one place. Some key organizers are shaped to keep all your keys together for better portability, while others serve as storage for easy access to everyone in the family. When you buy this gadget, you need to check if there's enough space for all your keys, but if you 3D print it, you'll get one with the exact specifications that you need.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts,’ and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts,’ and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title_orig: Violent protests multiply across Europe
articles.title_zh: Violent protests multiply across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Student protests in France are into their second month , escalating into demonstrations across Europe.
What began in September in France with pupils protesting against overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages has grown into wider anger at the cost of living and planned cuts to public services.
Protesters in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain have also taken to the streets over the lack of affordable housing, rising costs and failing public services – with many young people saying they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.
Facing their anger are leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron , Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez and Portugal’s PM Luis Montenegro. Sanchez belongs to the left, Meloni to the right and Macron and Montenegro are conservative-leaning centrists. But while their politics vary, they all face mounting unrest because of soaring costs of living.
Are they out of touch with the experiences and sentiments of youth in their countries? Al Jazeera visualises how prices, wages, housing and education have changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over the past 26 years, from when Macron, Meloni, Sanchez and Montenegro were in their 20s, much like many of the protesters angry with them.
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
Spain recorded the steepest increase at 78 percent, followed by Portugal at 71 percent, 68 percent in Italy and France at 59 percent.
That means goods and services that cost 100 euros ($112) in 2000 now cost about 178 euros ($200) in Spain, 171 euros ($192) in Portugal, 168 euros ($188) in Italy and 159 euros ($178) in France.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy, 8.3 percent in Spain, 8.1 percent in Portugal and 5.9 percent in France, the highest rate in all four countries since at least 2000.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By October that year, eight months into the war, energy prices across the eurozone were almost 42 percent higher than a year earlier, and food prices were also rising sharply, according to Eurostat .
Between 2021 and 2023, prices increased by 12 to 15 per cent in the four countries. Wages failed to keep up, and because prices do not fall back once inflation eases, many households are still feeling the squeeze today.
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 per cent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 per cent in Spain, 11 per cent in France and 20 per cent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.
In Spain most new jobs were in tourism and services, and were often seasonal and poorly paid,  Jaime Velazquez, a journalist in Madrid, told Al Jazeera’s Inside Story .
Julius Fintelmann, cofounder and editor-in-chief of The European Correspondent, said ageing societies were squeezing out opportunities for younger workers, adding that the pay gap between older and younger workers has been widening across high-income economies for decades, so the promise that each generation would be better off than the last no longer holds.
Housing has become harder to afford in all four countries since 2000, according to the OECD’s price-to-income ratio. It provides a broad picture of how house prices have changed relative to incomes over time. When prices rise faster than incomes, the ratio goes up, suggesting homes are becoming less affordable on average.
However, it doesn’t show which households or regions are hit hardest, does not account for mortgage and borrowing costs, and says nothing about the quality of the homes people are paying for.
Spain has seen the biggest change. Its price-to-income ratio is 56 per cent higher than in 2000, even after falling sharply following the 2008 financial crisis.
In France, the ratio is 39 per cent higher than in 2000, though it has eased slightly since peaking in 2022.
Italy is the exception where house prices have broadly kept pace with incomes, leaving the ratio just 5 per cent higher than in 2000.
Portugal has seen the sharpest change in recent years. Its price-to-income ratio fell steadily for 15 years after 2000, meaning homes became more affordable. But since 2015 the ratio has risen by 67 per cent.
The OECD publishes the price-to-income ratio with 2015 as its reference year. To compare it with the wage and price data in this article, which started in 2000, Al Jazeera has reset the figures so that 2000 = 100.
Education has been at the heart of the unrest in France, where protests began because of overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. While in Belgium and Albania, demonstrators have rallied against the rising cost of education and access to universities.
According to the latest data from Eurostat , France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.6 per cent in 2000.
Italy spent 4.4 per cent of its GDP on education compared to 4 per cent in 2024, Spain spent 4.1 per cent in 2000 and the same in 2024. Portugal spent 4.8 per cent in 2000 and 4.3 per cent in 2024.

The USDA released images of the packages subject to a recall by Kayem Foods Inc. of approximately 1.5 million pounds of meat products and included brands such as AlFresco, Kayem, and McKenzie, among others. (Source: USDA)
A Massachusetts company recalled more than 1.5 million pounds of ready-to-eat meat and poultry products that were produced over the past eight months after determining that they may not have been stored properly.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture posted the recall by Kayem Foods Inc., along with a list of scores of affected products. In addition to its own branded products, Kayem pulled items made under Al Fresco, McKenzie, and multiple other brands. (See lists below.)
The recalled products were manufactured over an eight-month span that stretches from March 31, 2026, to Oct. 7, 2026, and sent to stores and food service companies across the United States, as well as in Hong Kong, the statement on the USDA website indicated.
The affected items will have the establishment numbers "EST. M/P 7839," "EST. P 20935A" and "EST. M 9520" inside the USDA mark of inspection, it noted. See slideshow for images of the packaging of the recalled products.
RELATED: New protein ranking names unexpected winner over beef, salmon and eggs
The USDA released images of the packages subject to a recall by Kayem Foods Inc. of approximately 1.5 million pounds of meat products and included brands such as AlFresco, Kayem, and McKenzie, among others. (Source: USDA)
The USDA website explained that the recall was triggered after a customer complained about a product being warm when it was delivered at the beginning of October. An investigation revealed that some of the company’s meat and poultry products were stored in a warehouse cooler where the temperature had deviated from where it was supposed to be.
While the USDA is not aware of any illnesses linked to the products, its Food Safety and Inspection Service is concerned that the items may still be sitting in customers’ refrigerators. It advises anyone who finds one of the packages to throw it out or return it to its place of purchase.

articles.title_orig: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.title_zh: 4 Cool New Features Your Fitbit Air Is Getting In October 2026
articles.content_orig:
While the new Fitbit Edge is set to release in late October, the older Fitbit Air remains one of the best affordable fitness trackers you can buy today . It doesn't offer the same experience as a full smartwatch, but the Fitbit Air's comfortable build and versatile set of health and wellness tracking features make it a great alternative to Whoop and other screenless fitness bands.
While the Fitbit Air already comes with most features you'd want from a fitness tracker, Google recently announced several additions and improvements coming alongside the Fitbit Edge later in the month. These include the ability to passively track blood pressure trends, insulin resistance levels, and sleep breathing quality, which are all part of Google's new AI-based Health Guardian suite. Existing features like automatic workout detection are also being improved, and Google has also announced several partnerships with other health organizations to offer cross-platform compatibility with a variety of third-party services, devices, and apps. Some of these features are already rolling out, while users can expect others closer to the end of the month.
The American Heart Association labels hypertension (high blood pressure) as a 'silent killer' due to its lack of apparent symptoms until detected through screening. With nearly half of the adult population in the U.S. suffering from hypertension and being at risk of a heart attack or other health complications, monitoring blood pressure is extremely important — and Google is making it convenient for those with a Fitbit Air.
Google's new Health Guardian suite of features includes blood pressure trend tracking for users with a Google Health Premium subscription, which costs $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually. This uses the watch's optical heart rate and motion sensors alongside Google's WavesFM AI model to passively measure your blood pressure trends throughout the day and warn you of any risks on the first of every month. Google states that this isn't meant to replace a dedicated blood pressure measuring device, but it provides a proactive way to notice changes without having to visit a doctor. It's also worth noting that neither the Fitbit Air nor Google Pixel watches support on-demand blood pressure readings.
Blood pressure monitoring is nothing new in the wearable space. The 2021 Huawei Watch D offered background blood pressure tracking and on-demand measurements using a mechanical pump built into the watch, and U.S. owners of select Samsung Galaxy watches, such as the Galaxy Watch 9 (with an external pump), and owners of Apple wearables like the Apple Watch Series 12 also got the feature earlier this year. Google Pixel watches and the Fitbit Air were a notable exception until now.
Another frequently undetected condition that can pose severe risks is insulin resistance or impaired insulin sensitivity. Insulin regulates blood sugar by aiding cells in the absorption of glucose to produce energy, and consistent resistance to it can lead to conditions like prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes, as well as other health complications.
Google is adding insulin resistance monitoring to the Fitbit Air with Health Guardian for users with Google Health Premium. This uses data gathered throughout the month from many of the sensors already in the Fitbit — optical heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, and an accelerometer — and warns you of any detected trends that may present potential risks. Until now, only the Google Pixel Watch 5 had this feature, and now the Fitbit Air is also set to receive it. However, note that this feature only provides trend data and cannot provide on-demand insulin or blood glucose levels.
Beyond the newly added health metrics coming with Health Guardian, Google has also greatly improved certain existing features. If you've ever forgotten to start tracking a workout on your Pixel Watch or Fitbit Air, you might've noticed that it often intelligently does so without any manual input. The feature responsible for this is automatic activity detection, which is getting a huge upgrade in October.
Google states that automatic activity detection is going to be twice as accurate. This is possible using an AI model that will analyze context, such as your daily habits, when and how you work out, and manually added data. The number of supported workouts has also been expanded: the feature could initially detect only 10 activities, a number that has now been increased to over 100. The updated list of workouts includes swimming, strength training, certain racket and team sports, and more.
The Fitbit Air is a capable fitness band, but a standalone wrist-based tracker can only do so much by itself. You'll ultimately have to rely on other apps and equipment for specialized measurements, and managing different sources of data can be annoying. Fortunately, Google partners with several third-party health platforms and gives users the ability to sync and import data from a variety of apps and devices.
For instance, users with an Abbott Lingo continuous glucose monitor will soon be able to sync data with Google Health on select Google wearables, including the Fitbit Air. MyFitnessPal Premium users will now also be able to share food-specific logs with Google Health, and your Fitbit Air will get the ability to import lab results directly from Function Health later in the year. Starting early next year, users will also be able to sync Flo Health data with their Fitbit Air to receive more personalized advice from the Google Health Coach.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew.
The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial.
The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences.
But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal.
Military courts said he had no such authority but, in an August ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in favor of the government , prompting the men to appeal to the Supreme Court.
They argued, among other things, that the appeals court had no authority to intervene in the case.
The long delay in Mohammed facing trial was caused partly by concerns about evidence obtained via CIA torture.
A fourth alleged plotter earmarked for trial, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, was not involved in the appeal.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: 5 Ugreen Travel Gadgets Worth Adding To Your Long-Haul Flight Kit
articles.content_orig:
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Long-haul flights can be as tiresome and boring as they are exciting. Spending hours on a flight and at airports requires preparation to ensure you not only have fun during travel but also arrive at your destination with your phones and other devices topped up. This includes creating the perfect flight kit with tech gadgets like a long-lasting, TSA-approved power bank , a good set of noise-canceling headphones , an international travel adapter, and even tracking tags for peace of mind about the security of your prized possessions during your trip.
Luckily, you can find all these essential travel gadgets in one place: Ugreen. The popular consumer electronics brand sells a wide variety of charging accessories, as well as audio equipment and location trackers. That said, because it has a large library of products, it can be slightly confusing to know which ones to pick before you catch your next flight.
But we're here to help you. We've used our experience testing and comparing tech accessories to identify the top five Ugreen gadgets worth adding to your long-haul flight kit. These include a 20,000 mAh fast-charging wired power bank , a 10,000 mAh wireless power bank, a pair of over-ear headphones, and Ugreen's AirTag-like tracker tags. Even better, they're all budget-friendly and easily available on Amazon.
The Ugreen Nexode 20,000 mAh power bank is an ideal option for long-haul flights, even those that include long layovers. Its massive battery capacity means you can charge your devices multiple times before the power bank itself needs a recharge. According to Ugreen itself, the power bank can top up the iPhone 16 Pro 3.7 times, the Galaxy S25 Ultra three times, and even heavier-duty tech gadgets like the iPad Pro and MacBook Air more than once. At the time of writing, this budget-friendly power bank is available on Amazon for just $59.99, with a very strong 4.4-star rating after more than 5,500 reviews.
Another big selling point of this Ugreen power bank is its charging speed. It can deliver power at 100 W through its main USB-C outlet, which can juice up nearly any phone from 0% to 50% in less than half an hour. It also comes with a USB-C cable capable of supporting 100 W fast charging, so you don't have to spend extra. It's also got two other outlets: another USB-C with a 30 W output and one USB-A port with 22.5 W max output. In total, you can simultaneously charge three devices. Just note that in that case, the main USB-C port caps out at 65 W, which is still plenty fast.
Users also like how lightweight and compact this power bank is. It measures 5.47 by 3.23 by 1.02 inches and weighs just 0.925 pounds. One reviewer said, "it fits comfortably in a backpack and will charge multiple devices quickly." Lastly, we also like that the power bank itself charges quickly. It can charge at 65 W, going from nil to full in around two hours, according to Ugreen.
Although Ugreen is popular for its battery packs, docks, chargers, and other related accessories, it's also got a healthy lineup of headphones and earbuds. And the Ugreen HiTune Max5c wireless over ear headphones are a particularly great gadget for frequent flyers , thanks mainly to their value for money. They're priced at just $35.99 on Amazon, where they enjoy a solid 4.4-star rating after more than 2,200 reviews. According to expert hands-on testing at Hi-Tech.UA , their "sound is exactly at the level of models twice as expensive," while one everyday reviewer said that they're "similar quality to headphones that cost over $200."
They rock a 40 mm dynamic driver and offer punchy bass and surprisingly crisp highs. They're also certified to support Hi-Res audio, thanks to LDAC decoding, which reduces audio loss and latency during wireless transmission. Moreover, these are also noise-canceling headphones. They feature adaptive ANC with multiple modes, including complete isolation — Ugreen says its AI noise-canceling chip can reduce 43 dB of noise — and a transparency mode, giving you greater control over your surroundings. They can both dampen and totally eliminate the chatter around you during flights.
They also provide a comfortable fit. They've got a thick headband, big ear cushions that are made of soft leather and are easy to rotate (90-degree internal rotation and 15-degree external rotation) and extend, and a metal frame that makes them flexible yet robust. Despite their voluminous appearance, though, they weigh just 0.58 pounds, making them easy to wear for long periods. One reviewer said, "I watched two movies on the plane back to back with no pain." Lastly, the battery life is also great, at 75 hours with ANC off and 45 hours with ANC on.
Ugreen's FineTrack Mini 2 are small tracking devices that let you monitor the live location of your precious belongings, whether it's the hand luggage you take with you in the airplane cabin or your suitcases that often become difficult to find in that crowded conveyor belt, as well as other things like your wallet and keys. A pack of four (iOS only) currently costs just $31.99 on Amazon, with a 4.4-star rating after over 500 reviews. Even better, your purchase includes a keychain attachment case for each of the four air trackers.
One of their biggest pros is that they're compatible with Apple's Find My app , so you don't have to install any third-party application. Moreover, setup is seamless and straightforward. All you have to do is open Find My and add it as an object. And if you're running iOS 17 or later, you also have the ability to share the tracker's location with others. In addition to a long battery life of 5-7 years, they're also built to be easily found in the dark, courtesy of their fluorescent design.
They have an IP68 rating, so they can withstand harsh outdoor conditions, including heavy rain. We also like their alert system, which sends notification to you in the event your item has moved a bit too far. There's also an alarm feature, which produces loud 110 dB sounds at the press of a button to help you locate the tracker when it's nearby. One reviewer remarked that they're even louder than Apple's AirTags and called them "hands down a better buy than AirTags." For context, a pack of four AirTags costs around $99 — about thrice the price of Ugreen's air trackers.
A wireless power bank is the perfect fit for when you want to charge your phone on the flight without having to clutter your tray space with wires. The Ugreen MagFlow 10,000 mAh Qi2 wireless power bank , then, is worth your attention. It's compatible with the latest Qi2.2 wireless charging standard and can therefore charge any iPhone from iPhone 16 onward at 25 W, which is the fastest possible wireless charging speed available in Western markets right now. That equals 0-50% on the iPhone 17 Pro Max in around 38 minutes. It can also charge an iPhone 12-15, albeit at 15 W.
Right now, it's available on Amazon for $64.99, with a 4.5-star rating after more than 2,200 reviews. It comes with 17 magnets for easy snaps and solid grip. One reviewer said, "The magnetic hold is excellent. It stays securely attached to the phone and does not slide around." It can also function as a typical wired power bank, as it has two USB-C outlets capable of delivering 30 W of power output. One of them is the integrated USB-C cable that also functions as a carrying strap.
The power bank recharges at 30 W, meaning it'll take around two hours for a full recharge. Users also like the little display it comes with. "[It] helps keep track of how much juice we have left to squeeze," as one Amazon reviewer put it. It also has light indicators to show when wireless and fast charging are on or off. Additionally, it's convenient to carry around with you on flights. That's because it weighs just 0.56 pounds and measures 4.36 by 2.72 by 0.83 inches.

articles.title_orig: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.title_zh: Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 fighters
articles.content_orig:
A Houthi missile attack on the al-AIam military camp in southern Yemen has killed at least 53 people, according to local authorities.
The Iranian-backed armed group launched three ballistic missiles on Monday at the camp in Shabwa governorate during a training exercise, a spokesperson for Yemeni government forces said.
Officials for the internationally recognised government and medical sources initially said at least 18 people were killed and more than 30 wounded when the strike hit the facility, where new security recruits were undergoing training.
Those numbers increased dramatically later on Monday, when the local authority in Shabwa said 53 people had been killed and 200 injured, news agencies reported.
The attack was carried out as fighting continued to rage across Yemen. The civil war between the Saudi-backed government and Houthis had eased after a 2022 truce, but the regional impact of this year’s US-Israel war on Iran reignited hostilities.
Fighting escalated rapidly when the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God – seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded with a counteroffensive and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-aligned group seized in 2014.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Aramco.
On Monday, Saudi authorities sent alerts to residents of the capital Riyadh warning of “a hostile aerial threat”.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, said those killed in Shabwa were new recruits and promised a “firm response”.
“Targeting recruits reflects the Houthi militia’s approach of resorting to terrorist attacks when under pressure,” he said.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
“The Houthis said the attack targeted what they called a ‘Saudi-backed’ military base, referring to Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces who are stationed at military camps across the country,” he said.
“The Houthis say they will continue to target those bases. Spokesperson Yahya Saree says anywhere with a Saudi-backed military presence will be considered a legitimate target.”
Earlier, Yemeni government forces said they targeted Houthi gatherings, vehicles and weapons in al-Aqroudh, al-Shaqab and al-Sarari, south of Taiz, which is suffering from fuel shortages and soaring prices.
